# Social Isolation and Falls Risk: Lack of Social Contacts Decreases the Likelihood of Bathroom Modification Among Older Adults With Fear of Falling

**Authors:** Anna C. Siefkas; Ellen P. McCarthy; Bruce Leff; Alyssa B. Dufour; Marian T. Hannan

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 2Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife, Boston, MA, USA | 3Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 4Division of Geriatric Medicine, Center for Transformative Geriatric Research, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD, USA | 5Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, MD, USA | 6Johns Hopkins School of Nursing, Baltimore, MD, USA

## Abstract

Fall prevention strategies exist, but little is known about factors that influence whether they are used. We assessed whether social isolation modifies the association between fear of falling (FOF) and bathroom environmental modification. Data were included from 2858 Medicare beneficiaries in the National Health and Aging Trends Study. FOF and social isolation were assessed at baseline (2011); new bathroom modifications were assessed 1-year post-baseline. Social network size was dichotomized as any versus no social contacts. Logistic regression assessed associations between FOF and bathroom modification. Effect modification between FOF and social isolation was assessed with multiplicative interaction terms. FOF was associated with increased odds of bathroom modification. We observed a statistically significant interaction between FOF and social isolation (p = 0.03). Among those with no social contacts, FOF was associated with reduced odds bathroom modification that did not reach statistical significance (OR 0.5, 95% CI 0.2–1.3).

## Background and Objectives

Falls are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among older adults; each year in the United States as many as one in three adults over the age of 65 experience a fall, and nearly 25,000 deaths are directly attributed to falls in this age group (Burns etal., 2016). Fear of falling (FOF) (Tinetti et al., 1990) is associated with an increased risk of experiencing falls (Friedman et al., 2002), and prior work has supported that the presence of FOF may help to identify individuals at high risk for falling (Lavedán et al., 2018). FOF is also associated with negative social consequences, including reduced life-space and, social and physical isolation (Auais et al., 2017; Zijlstra et al., 2007). In addition to evidence indicating FOF may lead to social isolation, prior research has supporting that social network size and composition may also impact whether older adults experience FOF, with reduced social network sizes associated with an increased risk of FOF (Dierking et al., 2016; Malini et al., 2016). Evidence also suggests a relationship between social isolation and an increased risk of falls themselves (Pohl et al., 2018). These observed associations may be related to issues of social support (Umberson et al., 2010). In particular, individuals who are isolated or have fewer social contacts may experience less support to encourage proactive fall prevention measures as compared to those with larger social networks.

Although little is known about how social factors may impact fall risk, several preventative measures are known to be effective in reducing the risk of falls. Effective fall prevention measures include exercise programs targeting strength and balance, treatment of underlying medical conditions that increase fall risk, and environmental modifications to reduce fall risk in the home (Gillespie et al., 2012; Tricco et al., 2017). Modifications to reduce fall risk in the bathroom are of particular importance, as slippery and wet surfaces have been frequently identified as associated with fall risk (Keglovits et al., 2020), and bathrooms have been cited as a common location for falls occurring in the home (Ng et al., 2021; Stevens et al., 2014). Further, falls occurring in the bathroom are estimated to be more than twice as likely to result in injury as falls occurring in other parts of the home (Stevens et al., 2014).

Given the complex associations previously reported on the impact of social support on the fall risk factor FOF and on fall outcomes, the aim of this study was to assess whether social network size modifies the relationship between FOF and the fall prevention measure of bathroom environmental modification. In particular, we examined whether the association between FOF and bathroom environmental modification differs between isolated and non-isolated older adults. Our study tested the hypothesis that social isolation would function as an effect modifier (VanderWeele, 2009) of the relationship between a known fall risk factor (here, FOF) and engagement in fall prevention. If social isolation is found to modify the likelihood that individuals with heightened fall risk due to FOF engage in fall prevention, it may be an important factor to consider when studying the uptake of fall prevention programs.

### Research Design and Methods

#### Population and Study Design:

We used data from the National Health in Aging Trends Study (NHATS) baseline survey in 2011 (Round 1, n = 8245) and first annual follow-up survey (Round 2, n = 6572) (Freedman & Kasper, 2019; NHATS Public Use Data. (Rounds 1 and 2), Sponsored by the National Institute on Aging (Grant Number NIA U01AG032947) through a Cooperative Agreement with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health., 2014). NHATS is a longitudinal, nationally representative survey of Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 and older sponsored by the National Institute on Aging (NIA U01AG032947) through a cooperative agreement with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. For participants who were unable to complete the survey on their own, a proxy familiar with the respondent’s health completed the survey. All protocols for NHATS data collection were approved by the Johns Hopkins University institutional review board, and all study participants or their proxy respondents provided written informed consent.

We included participants who responded to both the baseline and Round 2 surveys and excluded participants whose baseline survey data was missing any covariates included in our analysis (n = 918). Because this study is concerned with environmental modifications made to bathrooms for individuals, participants were excluded if they lacked valid data on bathroom modifications at both the baseline and follow-up survey or if the bathroom modifications were present at baseline (n = 2763). Further, we excluded participants lacking a private bathroom (n = 33) all of whom were residents of an assisted living or nursing facility with a shared bathroom environment. The final analytic sample consisted of 2858 individuals (Figure 1). To assess that these exclusion criteria did not introduce selection bias, we separately examined the distribution of relevant covariates in the analytic sample and the full NHATS cohort and visually inspected their similarity.

#### Ascertainment of Fear of Falling (Exposure):

In the NHATS survey, questions about falling were preceded by a definition of falling down, defined as “any fall, slip, or trip in which you lose your balance and land on the floor or ground or at a lower level.” FOF was assessed at baseline by asking whether participants had worried about falling down in the last month (yes/no). NHATS separately records missing data (where no answer was provided) from questions which were answered as “Don’t Know” or questions for which an answer was refused. For these analyses, answers of “Don’t Know” or “Refused” were treated as missing data.

#### Assessment of Social Isolation (Effect Modifier):

NHATS collects data on social network size through the question “looking back over the past year, who were the people you talked with most often about important things?” Data on up to 5 such social network members were collected for each person. To examine social isolation an effect modifier, we created a binary variable classifying a person’s social network as containing at least one social contact or no social contacts using this information. This variable was used as a single-item indicator to identify socially isolated versus non-isolated individuals.

#### Assessment of Bathroom Environmental Modifications (Outcome):

Bathroom modification was assessed at the 1-year follow-up. At each survey, participants or proxy respondents were asked whether the participant’s home had each of the following: shower grab bars, bath seats, toilet grab bars, or raised toilet seats. For each outcome, we considered participants to have made environmental modification if the item was listed as not present at baseline and present at the follow-up survey. Similarly, we considered the modification to be absent if the item was not listed as present at either survey. We created a composite bathroom modification outcome variable where those who added at least one bathroom modification were considered to have the modification outcome.

#### Assessment of Covariates:

We considered demographic and health variables as potential confounders a priori, variables which we considered to be potential common causes of both FOF and home environmental modification based on prior literature and on clinical knowledge (Tinetti, 2003). Demographic variables of interest were age (grouped in 5-year intervals, with one category for those over 90), gender, race (White non-Hispanic, Black non-Hispanic, other non-Hispanic, or Hispanic), and whether the participant lived alone (yes/no). Health-related covariates included falls in the year prior to baseline, self- or proxy-reported presence of Alzheimer’s/dementia, arthritis, osteoporosis, use of any mobility device, and self-rated health (excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor). All potential confounders were evaluated at the baseline survey.

#### Descriptive statistics:

Frequencies and weighted percentages of demographic and health-related variables were examined by FOF status to allow for comparison of relevant characteristics between those with FOF and without FOF. Formal statistical tests between those with and without FOF were not performed. We similarly examined the distribution of social network size and presence of any bathroom modification at follow up by FOF.

#### Statistical analysis:

Because this study assessed the role of social isolation as a potential effect modifier of the relationship between FOF and subsequent environmental modification, all models included an interaction term between FOF and the social isolation indicator variable to assess effect modification on the multiplicative scale. We used logistic regression to examine the relationship between FOF at baseline and subsequent environmental modifications at the 1-year follow-up. Unadjusted models contained the main effect of interest (FOF) and the effect modifier (social network size) and their interaction. Adjusted models were adjusted for demographic and health related confounders. Odds ratios were calculated as in Supplemental Table 1.

We performed several independent sensitivity analyses. First, in order to assess the effect of how social network size was dichotomized, we ran the analysis after re-defining isolated vs. non-isolated status in two ways: (1) as two or more social contacts versus zero or one social contacts, following Cudjoe et al. in defining two or more social contacts as an “adequate” social network size (Cudjoe et al., 2020) and (2) as three or more vs. fewer than three social contacts, to assess the potential effects of relatively large social networks. Second, we performed an analysis limited to those living in the community by (1) excluding those patients who moved into any type of assisted living facility between the baseline and follow-up surveys and (2) excluding those patients who lived in any type of facility during the baseline and follow-up surveys. Focusing on these subsamples excludes those patients for whom environmental modification decisions may have been made for them by facility policy. Finally, because income was unavailable for approximately 40% of the sample, we repeated the primary analysis, as well as the sensitivity analyses that redefined the social network variable, on the subsample for which income data was available.

All analyses used SAS 9.4 survey procedures (Cary, NC) to adjust for the complex sampling design of NHATS, and results are weighted to reflect national estimates (Kasper & Freedman, 2019).

## Results

Table 1 depicts the characteristics of the analytic sample at baseline by FOF status. In general, those who reported a FOF at baseline were more likely to be older, to be female, to live alone, to have experienced a fall prior to baseline, to use a mobility device, and to self-report poor health, arthritis, or osteoporosis. The distribution of social network sizes was similar between the two groups, with the majority of respondents reporting 1 or 2 social network contacts in both groups. The analytic sample also showed a very similar distribution of covariates as compared to the NHATS full cohort with the exception of Alzheimer’s/dementia, which was approximately twice as prevalent in the full sample as compared to the analytic sample (Supplemental Table 2), though not highly prevalent in either sample (<8% in all groups). Those who reported FOF at baseline were also more likely to acquire home environmental modifications at the 1-year follow-up.

Table 2 presents unadjusted and adjusted associations between FOF, social isolation, and bathroom modification. Of the 2858 participants who were included in our primary analysis, 1515 (53%) had added some type of environmental modification to their bathroom environment. In the unadjusted analysis, FOF was only associated with future bathroom modification among those with at least one social contact (OR = 2.3, 95% CI 1.8–2.9). There was no association between FOF and bathroom modification among those with no social contacts and no association between social isolation and bathroom modification among those without FOF. The unadjusted interaction term was statistically insignificant (p = 0.18).

The fully adjusted analysis suggested that among those with no social network members, those with FOF had decreased odds of environmental modification at follow-up as compared to those without FOF (OR = 0.5, 95% CI 0.2–1.3). Having any social network members did not increase the odds of environmental modification as compared to having no social network members among those without FOF (OR = 1.1, 95% CI 0.7–1.7). However, those with FOF and with any social network members again had increased odds of environmental modification as compared to those without FOF and without any social network members (OR = 1.6, 95% CI 1.2–2.0), with a significant interaction term (p interaction= 0.03) (Table 3). It is worth noting that few survey participants reported a social network size of 0 (203 participants, 7.1% of analytic sample).

### Sensitivity Analyses

Table 3 depicts unadjusted and adjusted associations between FOF, social isolation, and environmental modification in a sensitivity analysis that dichotomized social network size as two or more versus zero or one. In the unadjusted analysis, FOF was statistically significantly associated with future bathroom modifications among those both with inadequate (<2 contacts) and adequate (2 or more contacts) social network sizes. Among those without FOF, adequate social network size was not associated with future bathroom modification (OR 1.1, 95% CI 0.9–1.3). The interaction term was similarly statistically non-significant (p = 0.72); those with both FOF and an adequate social network size had an OR of 2.2 (95% CI 1.6–2.9), which is negligibly different from the odds ratio in those with FOF and an inadequate social network size (OR = 2.3, 95% CI 1.8–3.0). In the adjusted analysis, FOF remained statistically significantly associated with bathroom modification as compared to those without FOF among those both with and without an adequate social network size (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1–1.8). Adequate social network size among those without FOF remained unassociated with bathroom modifications, and there was no evidence of effect modification between FOF and social network size (p = 0.91)

The remaining sensitivity analyses did not produce meaningfully different findings from the above analyses. Dichotomizing social network size as three or more versus less than three social network members did not meaningfully change the results in comparison to dichotomization as two or more versus zero or one. Limiting the sample to those living in the community did not meaningfully alter results of the primary analysis. In the subsample for which income data was available, controlling for income resulted in a smaller p-value (Supplementary Table 3). Controlling for income did not change the results of either sensitivity analysis that redefined the social network size dichotomization.

## Discussion and Implications

In this sample, we found that FOF is associated with an increased likelihood of bathroom environmental modification. In addition, there is evidence of significant effect modification by social isolation on this association. In particular, FOF decreased the odds of bathroom environmental modification among those with no close social contacts, although the association did not reach statistical significance. In contrast, those with FOF and at least one close social contact had increased odds of bathroom modification when compared to those with no FOF who were socially isolated. However, when social network size was dichotomized in ways other than any versus none, social network size does not meaningfully modify the association between FOF and bathroom environmental modification. These results support that the presence of any close social contacts may be an important factor in determining the likelihood of an individual with FOF engaging in fall prevention measures.

The present study adds to current knowledge by suggesting that social networks play an important role in understanding associations between fall risk and fall prevention. Previous literature has shown associations between social network characteristics and both FOF (Dierking et al., 2016; Malini et al., 2016) and fall risk (Pohl et al., 2018). Malini et al. report that FOF is significantly associated with a lack of available social support, with social support assessed via questions about the availability of friends, family, or neighbors who could care for the survey respondent if needed (Malini et al., 2016). Dierking et al. provide evidence that social network composition, as well as size, impact risk of FOF in a longitudinal cohort setting. Dierking et al. suggest that an increased number of non-familial social contacts is protective against developing FOF, while an increased number of familial social contacts increases the risk of FOF. They suggest that this may be due to the negative impacts of familial conflict (Dierking et al., 2016). Previous research in the NHATS population has also shown that social isolation, defined using indicators across the domains of marriage/partnership, family/friends, church participation, and club participation, is associated with an increased risk of falling (Pohl et al., 2018).

Our research adds to this body of work and provides evidence that the presence or absence of a social network may influence how likely those with FOF are to engage in fall prevention measures. As social networks have been reported to impact health outcomes and behaviors through a number of processes including social engagement and social influence (Kawachi & Berkman, 2001; Kelly et al., 2017; Kiely et al., 2000; Zunzunegui et al., 2003), the precise mechanisms underlying this associations merit further investigation. However, we hypothesize that social support provides a likely explanation (Kawachi & Berkman, 2001; Umberson et al., 2010). Social support can come in the form of instrumental support (e.g., money or labor), emotional support, or informational support, all of which may help encourage or enable individuals to engage in healthy behaviors (Umberson et al., 2010). Social support has been found to be associated with a decreased risk of FOF by Malini et al., as well as improved health outcomes in a variety of other settings, including improved survival after heart attacks (Berkman et al., 1992), decreased risk of depression among extended care facility employees (O’Donnell et al., 2011), and lower pain severity ratings in older adults after motor vehicle accidents (Richmond et al., 2018). Many of these associations may be due to social support enabling, encouraging, or implementing engagement in healthy behaviors.

In the present study, those with at least one social network member may be more likely to have the instrumental and informational support necessary to pursue and engage in fall prevention measures. Further, lack of social support may have contributed to the reduced odds of environmental modification associated with FOF among those with no social network members. FOF has been shown to be associated with reduced life-space (Auais et al., 2017); those with FOF may in fact be less able than their peers without FOF to engage in fall prevention measures without instrumental support provided by social contact members. While the existing literature supports this as a plausible explanation, few NHATS respondents in our study reported having no members of their social network, limiting the power of the present analysis. These results therefore require replication in a larger sample to confirm these findings.

There are several methodological strengths to this study. First, this study utilized a large and nationally representative study population, including often underrepresented segments of the older adult population, in particular racial minorities and participants over 90 years of age. Further, our analysis controlled for a range of important medical and socio-demographic confounders. This study also employed data with longitudinal follow-up; therefore, these results are not subject to concerns about reverse causality. Finally, this study also provided a wide range of sensitivity analyses to rigorously assess the assumptions underlying the primary analysis.

This study has several limitations. We were unable to differentiate between modifications that were acquired intentionally as compared to modifications that were acquired incidentally when the participant moved residences. Therefore, some of the newly acquired modifications may have been acquired incidentally, and not as fall prevention measures, which may have introduced a degree of misclassification of the outcome to this analysis. However, this misclassification is likely nondifferential, if present, and therefore would likely bias results closer towards the null. This study examined only social network size as a marker of social isolation and did not examine other important aspects of social networks, such as their overall composition; social network composition has been shown to impact the degree of social support received by social network contacts (Spitze & Logan, 1990). We also did not incorporate any measure of how involved each social network member was in the survey respondent’s life. We therefore did not capture potentially meaningful differences between one very involved contact as compared to several more distantly involved contacts. Social engagement outside the home was also not examined in this study. Future work incorporating these social factors would help to create a more nuanced understanding of the potential mechanisms by which social networks impact fall risk and fall prevention engagement. This study also considered bathroom environmental modification as a proxy for engagement with fall prevention measures, but does not directly assess other fall prevention measures. Future research should directly assess different types of fall prevention, such as exercise interventions, medication review, or treatment of conditions increasing fall risk, as the factors influencing uptake may differ for types of programs not studied here (e.g., ones completed outside the home). Research focusing specifically on individuals with no social network contacts may also prove valuable in determining the factors that influence fall prevention uptake in this high-risk population.

Despite these limitations, this study is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to directly assess the presence of effect modification between social isolation and FOF on the outcome fall prevention, as measured by the presence of home environmental modification. Our results suggest that the presence or absence of any social network may modify the effect that FOF has on engagement with fall prevention through home environmental modification. This finding may help to identify populations at an increased fall risk and who would benefit from additional support in addressing fall prevention.
